+ Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The red light makes everything sacred. It’s the first thing I learned in this class—how the darkroom’s glow strips away pretense, leaving only shadows and the slow bloom of images on paper. Right now, it’s stripping away something else. Elliot is across from me, his back against the counter, knees pulled to his chest. He’s wearing this oversized black cardigan with silver thread woven through it, thrifted no doubt, and his nail polish is chipped. A deep, wine-red. I noticed it three hours ago when he first walked in, and I’ve been trying not to stare since. “I don’t know how to say this,” he says, voice barely above a whisper. The developing trays slosh gently in the silence. “So I’m just going to say it.” I set down my tongs. My heart does this stupid little stutter, and I hate it. I’m Dani. I’m the one who makes the first move, who knows what she wants, who doesn’t do uncertainty. But with him, it’s different. It’s been different since the first day he walked into class with a vintage polaroid camera and a quietness that felt like a held breath. “Say it,” I say, softer than I mean to. He looks at me, and the red light catches the fear in his eyes. “I’ve been thinking… about gender. About how I present. And I think I might be—I don’t know if I’m trans, or non-binary, or just… something else. I don’t know what I am.” He laughs, a hollow sound. “I’m nineteen and I feel like a stranger in my own skin.” The words land between us like exposed film hitting the floor. I want to reach out and grab them, hold them up to the light, examine them. But I don’t. I stay still. “Okay,” I say. He blinks. “Okay?” “Yeah. Okay.” I shrug, trying to seem casual even though my pulse is hammering. “You don’t have to know. You’re allowed to not know.” It’s the right thing to say, but it’s also a lie. Because I *need* to know. I’ve spent the last four months cataloguing his eyelashes, the way he chews on his lip when he’s thinking, the way he moves through the world like he’s apologizing for taking up space. And now he’s telling me that the person I’ve been drawn to is becoming someone else, or maybe always was someone else, and I don’t know what that means for me. I’m attracted to men. Defined, masculine, solid. That’s my type. That’s what I know. Elliot was that—soft-spoken, sure, but undeniably a boy. A beautiful, quiet boy with a sharp mind and a gentle laugh. Now he’s telling me he might not be a boy at all, and I’m left standing on shifting ground. “I’m scared,” he says, pulling his knees tighter. “I’m scared that if I tell people, they’ll look at me differently. That I’ll lose something. That I’ll lose myself.” I move closer. Not too close—I don’t want to crowd him—but close enough that he can see my face clearly in the dim light. “You won’t lose yourself,” I say. “You’re finding yourself. That’s different.” He looks at me, and there’s something raw in his expression, something grateful and terrified all at once. “You’re the first person I’ve told.” That hits me harder than I expect. A warmth spreads through my chest, and I have to fight the urge to take his hand. My usual playbook—flirt, tease, take control—feels wrong here. Obscene. He’s not a conquest. He’s a person, trembling on the edge of becoming, and I want to be the one who holds the space for him. “Thank you,” I say. “For trusting me.” He smiles, small and fragile. “You’re easy to trust. You’re so… sure of yourself.” I want to laugh. Because I’m not sure of anything right now. I’m not sure who he’s becoming, or who I am in relation to it, or what this means for the way I see the world. But I can’t tell him that. Not now. He needs me to be steady. “I’m not as sure as I look,” I admit. “But I’m sure about this.” I gesture between us. “I’m sure I want to be here. With you. Whatever that means.” He exhales, and some of the tension leaves his shoulders. “I don’t know what I want,” he says. “I don’t even know what I look like yet. I’m trying to figure it out.” “That’s okay.” I reach out, finally, and let my fingers brush his knee. “You don’t have to figure it out alone.” The air between us shifts. It’s charged, electric, the way it gets right before a photo develops. I can see the outline of something forming, but I can’t tell what it is yet. I’ve never been good at waiting for the image to emerge. I always want to rush the process, to force it into focus. But with him, I want to wait. I want to see what he becomes. “Can I show you something?” he asks, and his voice is steadier now. I nod. He reaches into his bag and pulls out a stack of photo paper—unexposed, blank. He holds it up, and I watch as he takes a pen from his pocket and starts to write on the glossy surface. I can’t read it from here, but I can see the careful way he moves, the way his tongue pokes out slightly as he concentrates. When he’s done, he holds it out to me. The red light makes it hard to read, but I squint and make out the words: *I am becoming.* My throat tightens. “Elliot.” “I don’t know what comes next,” he says. “But I wanted to write it down. To make it real.” I hand the paper back to him, but he shakes his head. “It’s for you. So you remember.” I take it, careful, like it’s something precious. And it is. It’s a piece of him, this new version of him, and he’s giving it to me. “I’m not going anywhere,” I say. “I want to see who you become.” He smiles, and this time it reaches his eyes. “You’ll be the first to know.” We sit in the silence for a moment, the red light painting us in the same shade. And then I hear it—the soft *snap* of something falling. I look down and see the stack of photo paper he’d set on the counter, now lying on the floor, exposed to the faint light leaking under the door. “Shit,” he says, scrambling to pick it up. “It’s ruined,” I say, but I’m not upset. “The whole stack.” He looks at me, guilty. “I’m sorry. That was our last batch.” I shake my head. “It’s fine. We’ll get more.” But he’s already laughing, a real laugh this time, and I can’t help but join him. It’s absurd—this sacred moment, broken by a clumsy accident. And yet, somehow, it feels right. Like we needed the interruption to remind us that we’re still here, still human, still fumbling through the dark. “I guess we’re done for tonight,” he says. “Yeah.” I stand, and he does too. We’re close now, close enough that I can see the flecks of gold in his eyes. “But we’ll pick this up tomorrow. Same time?” He nods. “Same time.” I want to kiss him. I want to pull him close and tell him that whatever he becomes, I’ll be there. But I don’t. Because he’s not ready, and I’m not sure I am either. Instead, I touch his shoulder, light, and say, “I’m glad you told me.” He looks at me, and in the red light, I see it—the first glimmer of who he’s becoming. And I realize, with a jolt, that I’m excited to meet them. “Me too,” he says. We step out of the darkroom together, into the harsh fluorescent light of the hallway. And for the first time all night, I can see him clearly. He’s still Elliot. But he’s also something more. Something new. And I’m not scared. For the first time, I’m not scared at all.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The author successfully creates an intimate, contemplative atmosphere using the darkroom setting as both literal space and metaphor for self-discovery and uncertainty. The red light motif is effectively woven throughout, serving as a unifying visual element that reinforces the themes of development and revelation. The characterization of Dani is particularly well-executed. Her internal conflict between her usual assertiveness and her desire to give Elliot space feels authentic and psychologically complex. The author captures her confusion about her own identity and attraction without making it feel forced or overly dramatic. Dani's voice remains consistent throughout - thoughtful, slightly vulnerable beneath her confident exterior, and genuinely caring. Elliot's revelation is handled with appropriate sensitivity and realism. The dialogue feels natural and unforced, particularly in the tentative way he shares his uncertainty about gender identity. The author avoids making this a dramatic coming-out scene and instead presents it as a quiet, intimate moment of trust-building. The prose quality is generally strong, with effective use of sensory details and metaphor. The darkroom imagery works on multiple levels without being heavy-handed. Sentences flow well and the pacing feels appropriate for the contemplative mood. However, there are some areas where the writing could be stronger. The ending feels slightly too neat and optimistic given the complexity of the situation established earlier. While the mutual understanding reached between the characters is touching, it perhaps resolves Dani's internal conflict too easily. The symbolic moment with the ruined photo paper, while thematically appropriate, feels somewhat contrived as a plot device. The piece occasionally veers toward telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining Dani's thought processes about attraction and identity. Some of the internal monologue could be more subtle. Additionally, while the emotional complexity is generally well-handled, there are moments where the writing becomes slightly overwrought in its attempts to capture the significance of the moment. The adherence to the prompt is excellent - the piece captures all the requested elements including the setting, character dynamics, and thematic concerns. The word count appears appropriate and the first-person perspective is maintained effectively throughout. Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Trevi Fountain roared its endless white noise, a liquid thunder against the honeyed stone. Ben, Dr. Benjamin Thorne, was lost. Not geographically—his map app was perfectly functional—but existentially. He was a man of dusty archives and precise footnotes, adrift in a city that pulsed with a life he couldn't catalogue. He clutched his guidebook, *Rome for the Discerning Traveler*, like a talisman, his head bowed as he navigated a paragraph on Baroque iconography. Alessandra saw him a second too late. Her Vespa, a battered silver stallion named *Vespa*, screamed as she swerved, the front wheel kissing the cobblestone a hair's breadth from his polished loafers. The air filled with the acrid smell of burnt rubber and her own, very specific, Roman curse. “*Cazzo!*” she spat, yanking her helmet off. Her dark hair, a riot of waves, escaped its confines. “You have a death wish, *straniero*? Or do you simply wish to be a fresco on my fender?” Ben stumbled back, his guidebook clattering to the ground. “I’m terribly sorry! I wasn’t looking—the fountain, you see, Bernini’s genius—I was quite absorbed.” He fumbled for the book, his face a mask of crimson apology. “Are you alright? I’m so dreadfully clumsy.” Alessandra’s sharp, dark eyes took him in: the rumpled linen shirt, the earnest, flustered face, the way he clutched his book as if it were a life raft. A slow, mischievous smile spread across her lips. “You are like a lost puppy. A very tall, very polite, lost puppy.” She gestured to her scooter. “You see this? This scar, here?” She pointed to a long, angry scratch along the side panel, a streak of raw metal against the silver paint. “That was a Vatican cardinal on a bicycle. He was not so polite. You are luckier than a cardinal.” Ben blinked, a laugh escaping him before he could stop it. “I… I’m not sure that’s a comparison I’ve ever heard.” “It is a good one,” she declared, her chin jutting out. She picked up his guidebook, glanced at the title, and scoffed. “*Discerning Traveler*? This is a book for people who are afraid of getting their shoes dirty.” She tossed it back to him. “Come. I will show you the real Rome. The one that bites.” It was an impulse, a whim born of boredom and the intriguing canvas of his flustered Englishness. Before he could protest, she had his hand in hers, her grip surprisingly strong, and was pulling him away from the fountain. “But my hotel—my research—” he stammered. “Your research can wait. Bernini will still be dead tomorrow,” she said, her laughter a bright, sharp sound against the fountain’s roar. Thus began Ben’s undoing. Scene 1: The Espresso Bar Alessandra dragged him into a cramped, fluorescent-lit bar where the air was thick with the scent of coffee and the shouts of old men playing cards. She ordered in rapid-fire Romanesco, a dialect that made Ben’s textbook Italian sound like a dying language. She slid a tiny, tar-black espresso across the counter to him. “Drink,” she commanded. He sipped. It was a bitter, violent explosion of flavor. He winced. “Good, yes?” she asked, her eyes dancing. “It’s… intense,” he managed. “That is Rome,” she said, downing her own in one swift gulp. As she turned to leave, her hand brushed a small, silver sugar bowl on the counter. In a motion so fluid it was almost invisible, the bowl disappeared into the folds of her leather jacket. Ben saw it. He blinked, certain he’d imagined it. She caught his gaze and winked, a silent, daring challenge. He felt a jolt, not of disapproval, but of thrilling, illicit complicity. Scene 2: The Pantheon’s Oculus They stood in the vast, cool interior of the Pantheon, a shaft of sunlight beaming down through the oculus. Ben was trying to explain the mathematical perfection of the dome, his voice reverent. Alessandra, however, was looking up, a calculating glint in her eye. “They say the rain comes in,” she mused. “And sometimes, rose petals, dropped from the top on Pentecost.” “It’s a remarkable feat of engineering,” Ben began. “It is a giant hole in the roof,” she countered, grinning. “The Romans are very good at making a beautiful mess.” She reached into her pocket and pulled out a small, smooth stone she’d picked up from the street. “Here,” she said, pressing it into his hand. “A piece of the mess. A souvenir from your first day of being alive.” He stared at the unassuming pebble, then at her. It felt heavier than it should. A token. A secret. Scene 3: The Trastevere Alley The sun was beginning its slow descent, painting the Tiber in hues of gold and amber. Alessandra led him down a narrow, laundry-strung alley in Trastevere. She stopped in front of a graffiti-covered metal door. “Ready for a real Roman experience?” she asked, her smile sharp. Before he could answer, she produced a small, worn key from her boot and unlocked it. Inside was a hidden courtyard, overgrown with jasmine, a broken fountain gurgling in the center. A few mismatched chairs were scattered around a rusted table. “My uncle’s,” she explained. “He’s in Sicily. We are trespassing.” “This is… illegal,” Ben whispered, his heart hammering against his ribs. “Only if we get caught,” she said, settling into a chair and patting the one beside her. “Tell me, *professore*, have you ever done anything truly bad?” He thought of his life—the safe, predictable trajectory of lectures, papers, and sabbaticals. “I once returned a library book three days late.” Alessandra threw her head back and laughed, a full, unguarded sound. “I once stole a Vespa from a man who looked at me the wrong way.” She gestured to the scooter parked outside. “Not that one. That one I stole from a man who looked at me the right way.” She winked again, and Ben felt the ground shift beneath him. Scene 4: The Sunset on the Gianicolo They ended up on the Janiculum hill, the city sprawled before them like a glittering, chaotic map. The dome of St. Peter’s glowed in the fading light. Ben was breathless, not from the climb, but from the sheer, relentless energy of the day. He had been robbed of his guidebook (she’d thrown it in a fountain, claiming it was “bad luck”), fed questionable street food, and had been an accessory to at least three acts of petty larceny. “You are a menace,” he said, but his voice was full of wonder. “I am a Roman,” she corrected, leaning against her Vespa. The scratch on its side caught the last of the sun’s rays. “We are born with a little bit of chaos in our blood.” He looked at her, this whirlwind of a woman with the stolen sugar bowl in her pocket and the ghost of a smile on her lips. He felt a profound, terrifying, and utterly wonderful sense of being unmoored. His carefully constructed world had been shattered, and in its place, she had built a chaotic, vibrant one, just for a day. “I have to go,” he said, the words feeling hollow. “My flight… I have a conference in Florence tomorrow.” Alessandra nodded, her expression unreadable. She reached into her jacket and pulled out the silver sugar bowl. She pressed it into his hands. “A souvenir,” she said, her voice softer now. “For your first day of being alive.” He looked at the bowl, then at her. He wanted to say something profound, to capture the feeling of vertigo and delight she had given him. But all he could manage was, “Will I see you again?” She straddled her Vespa, the engine coughing to life. She looked back at him, her dark eyes holding his for a long, charged moment. A slow, enigmatic smile touched her lips. “Rome is a small city, *professore*,” she said. “And I am a very good finder of lost things.” She revved the engine and shot off into the twilight, a silver blur weaving through the traffic. Ben stood on the hill, the stolen sugar bowl cold in his hand, the scent of her jasmine-scented courtyard still in his hair. He was disoriented, utterly captivated, and completely, hopelessly smitten. He had a feeling he was going to miss his conference in Florence. And for the first time in his life, he didn’t care.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and vivid storytelling within the contemporary romance framework. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through action and dialogue. Alessandra's mischievous energy and Ben's scholarly awkwardness are well-established and consistently maintained throughout. The narrative structure works effectively, using interconnected scenes that build momentum and deepen the relationship. The Roman setting is richly evoked through specific details like the Trevi Fountain's "liquid thunder," the cramped espresso bar, and the jasmine-scented hidden courtyard. The author demonstrates strong command of sensory details and atmospheric writing. The kleptomania subplot is handled with appropriate subtlety - the sugar bowl theft is witnessed but not explicitly discussed, creating complicity between characters and reader. This adds layers to Alessandra's character without making her unsympathetic. However, the piece suffers from occasional overwrought descriptions that border on purple prose. Phrases like "existentially lost" and "liquid thunder against honeyed stone" feel forced. The writing sometimes prioritizes lyrical language over natural expression, particularly in the opening paragraphs. The dialogue generally feels authentic, capturing Alessandra's directness and Ben's formal politeness, though some exchanges lean toward the theatrical. The cultural clash is well-rendered through speech patterns and attitudes. The emotional arc is believable - Ben's gradual loosening up feels earned through the accumulation of experiences rather than sudden transformation. The ending strikes an appropriate note of possibility without forcing resolution. Some scenes feel slightly rushed, particularly the Pantheon sequence, which could have been developed further. The pacing occasionally sacrifices depth for momentum, though this suits the whirlwind nature of the day. The piece succeeds in creating genuine chemistry between the protagonists and establishes a compelling foundation for a longer work. The writing demonstrates skill in character development, setting, and romantic tension, despite some stylistic excesses. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Vega whisky hits the glass with a soft, amber sigh. The stranger’s tentacled dreads, the color of bruised plums, are indeed askew, one of the sensory tips twitching like a startled anemone. I slide the double across the worn, polished bar-top, a surface scarred by a thousand mugs and a few knife fights. “Rough transit?” I ask, wiping down a spot that will never be clean. He downs half the glass in one gulp, his throat working in a way that’s both fascinating and slightly unsettling. He’s got four eyes, two large and two small, all of them fixed on the bar’s surface as if it holds the secrets to the universe. “Rough,” he croaks. “The kind of rough that makes you re-evaluate your life choices.” “Story of the Outpost,” I say, leaning my elbows on the bar. Behind me, a glass shatters. I don’t flinch. Jax, the resident bouncer and part-time glassware assassin, probably tried to catch a falling bottle. He’s built like a cargo hauler and has the grace of one, too. The sound is just background noise, the Outpost’s own heartbeat. The stranger, who hasn’t offered a name, stares into his glass. “Ever have a day where the universe decides to personally, actively, and maliciously screw you over?” His voice is a low, gravelly hum. “Honey, I’m a bartender. That’s my Tuesday.” I gesture to the mostly-empty bar. “But you look like you’ve had a week of Tuesdays. What’s your name?” He hesitates, his smaller eyes darting to the door, then back to me. “Kael. And I’m not looking for trouble. I’m looking for a way *out* of it.” “The Outpost’s a good place for that. We don’t ask too many questions, and the law is… negotiable.” I nod toward the far corner where a group of miners are arguing over a game of Stellar Poker. “As long as you don’t cheat at cards or spill a drink on the floor without buying the next round.” Kael lets out a humorless laugh. “My problem isn’t a card game. It’s… a cargo manifest.” He pulls a crumpled, greasy piece of data-paper from his jacket and slides it across the bar. I don’t touch it. I just look at it. It’s stamped with a symbol I recognize: a red, stylized claw. The Varnak Cartel. My stomach tightens. “You’re hauling for the Varnak?” “Was,” he corrects, his voice dropping to a whisper. “I was. But there was a… discrepancy. A mis-shipment. What I delivered to the refinery on Krel-7 wasn’t what the manifest said it was supposed to be.” “What was it supposed to be?” “Medical supplies. What it actually was, was a crate of… well, let’s just say it’s highly illegal, highly volatile, and the Varnak are *very* unhappy that it’s not where they thought it was.” I finally pick up the manifest, my eyes scanning the flowery, bureaucratic language. It’s a standard shipping form, but the cargo description has been altered. The original text is still faintly visible underneath. “This says ‘Stabilized Plasma Cells’. The correction says ‘Nova-Core Detonators’.” Kael nods miserably. “Someone swapped the crates at the last jump station. I didn’t check. I was running late, and my co-pilot… he was supposed to verify. Now he’s vanished, and the Varnak are blaming me. They think I’m trying to sell their detonators on the side.” I push the manifest back. “And you brought them here? To the Outpost?” “I didn’t have a choice! I can’t go back, I can’t jump forward, every port in this sector is either Varnak-owned or Varnak-fearing. This was the only place where a ship could land without a full customs scan.” He downs the rest of his whisky, and I pour him another without being asked. “The Outpost is neutral,” I say, but my mind is racing. “We don’t have customs. But we do have a manager, and she has a strict policy about attracting the attention of organized crime. It’s bad for business.” “I’m not asking for asylum,” Kael says, leaning forward, his four eyes finally meeting mine. “I’m asking for a place to stash the crate for one cycle. Just until I can figure out who set me up. I’ll pay. I have credits.” “It’s not about credits,” I say, and I mean it. “It’s about the fact that if the Varnak trace your ship here, they’ll come looking. And they won’t just ask for you. They’ll ask for everyone.” “I’m not a criminal,” he insists, his voice cracking. “I’m a freighter pilot. I haul legal goods. I have a daughter on Vesta Prime. I’m not throwing that away for a crate of bombs.” I look at him. His dreads are trembling, and his hand, wrapped around the glass, is shaking. He’s scared. Genuinely, bone-deep scared. I’ve seen that look before, on a dozen different faces, from a dozen different species. It’s the look of a person who’s realized they’re a pawn in someone else’s game. “What’s in the crate now?” I ask, my voice low. “It’s in my cargo hold, still sealed. I haven’t opened it.” “And you’re sure it’s detonators?” “The manifest says so. And the Varnak’s message said so.” He pulls out a small comm-device, its screen cracked. He plays a recording. A raspy, synthesized voice fills the air. *“Kael. You have one cycle to return our property to the designated coordinates. Failure to comply will result in the liquidation of your assets, beginning with your daughter on Vesta Prime. We know where she goes to school.”* The threat hangs in the air, cold and final. A silence falls over the bar, and even the miners in the corner stop their arguing to glance our way. I take a deep breath. This is a problem. A big, dangerous, galaxy-sized problem. And it’s sitting in my bar, drinking my whisky. “Okay, Kael,” I say, picking up his empty glass and placing it in the sink. “You’re in trouble. And I’m sorry about that. But the Outpost is my home. These people are my family. And I can’t let you bring a Varnak death squad to our doorstep.” His face falls. “So you’re throwing me out?” “I didn’t say that,” I say, a plan forming, half-baked and risky. “I said I can’t let you bring the death squad here. You said the crate is still in your hold. So, what if the crate was never here? What if your ship was searched by a neutral party, and the crate was confiscated and destroyed?” His smaller eyes widen. “That’s… that’s a lie.” “It’s a story,” I correct him. “And stories are what we sell here at The Last Outpost. But it needs a witness. It needs a piece of evidence. It needs someone to verify that the crate was, indeed, destroyed.” He looks at me, a flicker of hope in his four eyes. “Who?” I glance over at Jax, who is now carefully sweeping up the broken glass, his massive frame hunched over the broom. He catches my eye and gives me a slight nod. He’d heard everything. “You’re going to have to trust me,” I say, wiping the bar again. “And you’re going to have to trust Jax. And you’re going to have to pray that the Varnak are as stupid as they are ruthless.” “And if they’re not?” Kael asks. I don’t have an answer for that. The bell on the door jingles, and a cold draft sweeps in. A figure in a long, dark coat stands silhouetted in the doorway, and the hum of conversation in the bar dies instantly.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt requirements, delivering a cozy sci-fi story set in The Last Outpost with Nettle as the first-person narrator. The author successfully establishes conflict through Kael's predicament with the Varnak Cartel and stolen detonators, while appropriately leaving it unresolved. The dialogue ratio appears to meet the requested 60%, and the word count seems appropriate. The characterization is particularly strong. Nettle emerges as a believable bartender with a protective instinct toward her found family at the Outpost. Her voice is consistent throughout - pragmatic, experienced, and caring without being sentimental. Kael is well-developed as a desperate freight pilot caught in circumstances beyond his control, with specific details like his daughter on Vesta Prime adding emotional weight. The world-building feels lived-in and authentic. Details like Jax the clumsy bouncer, the scarred bar surface, and the casual mention of different species create a believable space station environment. The author avoids over-explaining the sci-fi elements, letting them emerge naturally through context. The prose strikes an effective balance between descriptive and functional. Phrases like "tentacled dreads, the color of bruised plums" and "amber sigh" add color without becoming overwrought. The writing maintains the cozy atmosphere while building genuine tension. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building the world. Nettle's bartender wisdom ("Honey, I'm a bartender. That's my Tuesday") rings true, as does Kael's desperation. The conflict escalation is well-paced, moving from personal trouble to threats against Kael's daughter to the ominous figure in the doorway. The stakes feel real and the tension builds organically. Some minor weaknesses include occasional exposition that could be more seamlessly integrated, and the ending figure's entrance, while dramatic, borders on slightly predictable thriller territory. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The saxophone finds me first. It curls out of the crowd like smoke, a low, mournful wail that slides between the chatter of tourists and the hiss of streetcar brakes. It’s not a happy sound. It’s the sound of a man who’s seen things and is trying to blow them out of his lungs. I get it. I’m standing on a corner in the French Quarter, and my backpack feels like it’s filled with bricks. Two states. I made it two states. The guy who picked me up outside Memphis—a trucker with a Jesus fish tattoo and a tin of chewing tobacco—had been fine. Quiet. He let me sleep in the passenger seat while the highway unspooled like a grey ribbon. He dropped me here, at the edge of a world that smells like beignets and stale beer and river water. He said, “You take care, kid,” and drove off. That was three hours ago. Three hours of just… standing. Watching. The sun is climbing higher, and the air is getting thick and wet, like breathing through a damp towel. I don’t have a plan. That’s the thing. My plan ended at "get out of dodge." I didn’t think about the after. There is no after. There’s just this. This loud, colorful, overwhelming *now* that doesn’t care that my name is Taylor and that my mom’s voice went all tight and weird when I told her, like I’d handed her a snake. She didn’t scream. That would’ve been better. She just said, “We’ll talk about this when you’re feeling more like yourself,” and then she went to make dinner, and the silence in that house was louder than any argument. My dad didn’t say anything at all. He just looked at me like I was a stranger who’d wandered into his kitchen. And now I’m here, and the saxophone is still crying, and a woman with a beaded headdress is trying to sell me a bracelet made of plastic pearls. “For luck, cher,” she says, her voice like molasses. I shake my head. I don’t want luck. I want a direction. I start walking. The street is packed. A mime is pretending to be trapped in a box. A juggler is tossing flaming torches. It’s all so aggressively *alive* that it makes my chest ache. I feel like a ghost. A ghost in a hoodie, sweating through my binder, my feet sore in my worn-out sneakers. I’m a ghost with a dead phone battery and forty-three dollars in crumpled bills. I’m thinking about finding a bus station, maybe a shelter, when I nearly trip over her. She’s sitting on the curb, legs crossed, drawing in a battered spiral notebook. She’s got a shock of purple hair, a nose ring, and a denim jacket covered in patches: band logos, a safety pin, a small rainbow flag. My heart does a stupid little flip at that. “Watch it,” she says, not looking up. Her voice is flat, bored. “Sorry,” I mumble. I start to walk away, but I stop. I don’t know why. Maybe because she’s the only person here who isn’t performing. She’s just… sitting. Like me. A stone in a river. “You lost?” she asks, finally looking up. Her eyes are a startling, pale blue. They’re sharp. They’re looking at me, not through me. It’s unsettling. “No,” I say. “Just… exploring.” She snorts. “Right. With a backpack that big and a face that scared? You’re either running from something or running to something. Which is it?” The question hits me like a slap. My throat tightens. I want to say, *Both. Neither. I don’t know.* Instead, I just shrug. She pats the curb next to her. “You look like you’re about to pass out. Sit.” I hesitate. Trust. My brain screams *danger*. This is how it happens, right? In the movies. The runaway meets the street-smart kid who’s actually a trafficker. But then she goes back to her drawing, and I see it’s a sketch of a bird, mid-flight, its wings spread wide. It’s good. Really good. And I’m so tired. Tired of thinking, tired of being on high alert, tired of the voice in my head that keeps replaying Mom’s silence. I sit. The concrete is warm through my jeans. “I’m Jules,” she says, not looking up. “Taylor.” “Taylor,” she repeats, testing it. “Cool. You staying long?” “I don’t know. I don’t have a place.” Jules finishes a line on the bird’s wing, then closes the notebook. She turns to face me fully. Up close, I see the dark circles under her eyes, the faint bruise on her jaw that she’s tried to cover with concealer. She’s older than me. Maybe nineteen. But she has that same look I feel in my own mirror: worn out, but still fighting. “You got any money?” “A little.” “Any friends here?” “No.” “Family?” I shake my head. The word *family* feels like a foreign object, something sharp I’ve swallowed. Jules nods, like she’s heard a hundred stories like mine. She probably has. “Okay. Look. I know a place. A squat over on Esplanade. It’s not the Ritz, but it’s dry, and the cops mostly leave us alone. There’s a few of us. We look out for each other.” I should say no. I should thank her and walk away and find a shelter. But the saxophone player has switched to a different tune now, something faster, almost joyful. It’s like the city is daring me to take a chance. And I’m so goddamn tired of being safe. Safe got me a silent house and a counselor’s smug face. Safe got me nothing. “Why?” I ask, my voice coming out smaller than I want. “Why would you help me?” Jules’s pale eyes hold mine. For a second, the mask slips, and I see something raw and scared underneath. “Because someone helped me once,” she says, quiet. “And I promised myself I’d pay it forward.” She stands up, brushing off her jeans. “You coming or what?” The saxophone wails. The crowd surges around us, a river of sound and color. I look at Jules, at the rainbow flag on her jacket, at the bird she just drew, frozen mid-flight. I don’t know if she’s a friend or a trap. I don’t know if this is the beginning of a new life or the end of this one. But I know I can’t stay on this curb forever. I stand up, shouldering my pack. “Yeah,” I say, and the word feels like a key turning in a lock. “I’m coming.” And for the first time in forty-eight hours, I take a step that isn’t just running away. It’s running *toward* something. Even if I don’t know what it is yet.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in portraying a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The backstory is woven in naturally through Taylor's reflections on their parents' reactions, avoiding heavy exposition dumps. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with some particularly strong metaphorical language ("silence in that house was louder than any argument," "a stone in a river"). However, the piece occasionally veers toward predictable territory - the meeting with Jules follows familiar runaway narrative patterns, and some descriptions border on overly poetic for the character's voice. The ending, while hopeful, feels slightly rushed in its emotional shift from despair to tentative optimism. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 78.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The morning light, the color of weak tea, bled through the corrugated iron roof of the old supermarket. Midas sat on a pallet of desiccated dog food, staring at the map spread across his knees. It was, in fact, a placemat from a defunct seaside chippy, but the stains had arranged themselves in a way that suggested topography. “The plan is simple,” he said, tapping a greasy smear that might have been the North. “We follow the old A-road for two days, then cut east through the woods. The message said ‘the smiling man will guide you.’ Simple.” Chewy, the animo-tronic koala, sat on the pallet beside him. His fur was a matted, greyish-white, and his eyes, two black plastic beads, held the profound, unblinking stare of a creature that had seen empires fall and had found the whole business mildly inconvenient. A small speaker in his chest emitted a low, mechanical hum. “The smiling man,” Chewy said, his voice a tinny, synthesized baritone. “Statistically, in the post-collapse world, a smiling man is either a hallucination, a trap, or a cannibal with very good dental hygiene. Our odds of a pleasant encounter are, I calculate, 0.04%.” “That’s a chance,” Midas said, folding the map with a decisive crinkle. “We’re low on batteries for you, and I’m tired of eating tinned peaches. They taste like regret. A hidden refuge might have a working vending machine.” “A vending machine,” Chewy repeated, the hum in his chest pitching slightly higher. “A machine that dispenses sustenance. A beautiful, illogical dream. Very well. But I am logging a formal objection. This is a fool’s errand.” “You always say that.” “And I am always right,” Chewy buzzed. “Remember the ‘Abandoned Armory’ that was a nest of giant hornets? Or the ‘Friendly Settlement’ that was a cult of people who worshipped a broken microwave?” “The microwave had a nice glow,” Midas muttered, shouldering his pack, which contained mostly duct tape and a single, precious roll of toilet paper. The day’s journey began with a promising stumble. Midas, navigating by the rusty skeleton of a crashed helicopter, tripped over a root and fell face-first into a patch of stinging nettles. The cursing was impressive. Chewy, strapped to his back, offered a running commentary. “Your spatial awareness is a marvel of negative engineering,” he said. “I am updating my internal map. We are now precisely zero meters closer to the smiling man.” They found the A-road, a cracked ribbon of tarmac being slowly devoured by brambles. They walked for an hour, the silence broken only by Midas’s grumbling and the occasional whirr of Chewy’s internal gyroscope. Then they saw it. A figure. It was a man, standing perfectly still in the middle of the road. He was wearing a faded suit and a wide, unsettling grin. Painted on his face was a crude, white smile, extending from ear to ear. “The smiling man,” Midas whispered, a surge of hope rising in his chest. “See? Not a trap.” “He is holding a machete,” Chewy observed. “And his grin is painted on. That is not a happy grin. That is a ‘I have a very specific plan for your internal organs’ grin.” The man raised the machete and took a step forward. Midas, with the coordination of a startled deer, turned and ran. He didn’t get far. His foot caught in a pothole, and he went down hard, rolling into a ditch filled with oily, stagnant water. Chewy, dislodged, flew from his back and landed with a splash, his mechanical limbs splayed. The smiling man stood over them, his painted grin unwavering. He opened his mouth, and a sound like a dying radio emerged. “Grrr-bzzzt. Welcome. Welcome to the Smile Zone.” “I told you,” Chewy gurgled from the water. “He’s a broken robot. Probably a security droid from the before times. His smile circuit is fried.” The droid’s machete swung. Midas, in a moment of pure, desperate genius, threw the roll of toilet paper. It unspooled in the air, a white ribbon of hope, and wrapped around the droid’s head, obscuring its vision. The droid staggered, swinging wildly. Midas scrambled out of the ditch, grabbed Chewy by one soggy ear, and ran. He didn’t stop running for what felt like an hour. They crashed through undergrowth, forded a stream that was more mud than water, and finally collapsed in a small clearing, panting. “My… circuits… are… damp,” Chewy wheezed. “The toilet paper. A noble sacrifice. I will add it to your list of ‘Almost Competent’ moments.” Midas lay on his back, staring at the sky. “We’re lost. We’re wet. And we have no toilet paper.” “The mission has been a resounding success,” Chewy said, his voice regaining some of its tinny sarcasm. “We have confirmed the existence of a hostile robotic cannibal, we have discovered a new and exciting way to get lost, and we have successfully depleted our most valuable resource. I estimate our survival probability has dropped to 0.01%.” Midas sat up and looked around. A rusted sign, half-buried in the undergrowth, caught his eye. It read: ‘MEGA-MART: 500m’. He could see the grey, hulking shape of a building through the trees. It was the same Mega-Mart they had left that morning. “Well,” Midas said, a grim smile on his face. “At least we know the way home.” They trudged back, a ragged, muddy duo. The sun was setting, casting long shadows. They found the hole in the fence they used as a back door. Inside, the supermarket was just as they’d left it. Midas slumped onto the pallet of dog food. Chewy, propped against a jar of pickles, let out a final, static-laced sigh. “The smiling man,” Chewy said, his voice a low buzz. “He was a metaphor, Midas. A metaphor for the universe’s desire to see you fail.” Midas opened a tin of peaches. “Tomorrow,” he said, taking a bite. “Tomorrow we map the other side of the car park.” Chewy’s eyes glowed faintly in the gloom. “Excellent. A new horizon of disappointment awaits.” The little koala’s speaker hummed, then went silent, leaving Midas alone with his peaches and the profound, unblinking certainty of a bad idea.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a solid understanding of Terry Pratchett's style, capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and philosophical undertones wrapped in absurdist situations. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic buddy comedy with genuine Pratchettesque elements: the matter-of-fact acceptance of bizarre circumstances, deadpan delivery of profound observations, and the universe's apparent malevolence toward hapless protagonists. The characterization is well-executed, particularly Chewy, whose sardonic commentary and statistical observations feel authentically robotic while maintaining personality. Midas embodies the classic Pratchett everyman - competent enough to survive but cursed with optimism that leads to predictable disasters. Their dynamic works well, with Chewy serving as both Greek chorus and voice of reason. The prose style captures Pratchett's rhythm effectively, with clever turns of phrase like "morning light, the color of weak tea" and "coordination of a startled deer." The author demonstrates skill in balancing humor with genuine tension and maintains consistent voice throughout. The plot structure follows the requested format perfectly - deliberation, mission gone wrong, return home worse off. The circular journey ending where they started reinforces themes of futility while avoiding genuine despair. The "smiling man" reveal as a malfunctioning security droid is both logical and absurd in appropriate measure. However, some elements feel slightly forced in their Pratchett imitation, particularly certain statistical observations from Chewy that don't quite land with the master's precision. The toilet paper solution, while creative, borders on convenient coincidence. Some descriptive passages, while competent, lack the effortless elegance of Pratchett's best work. The dialogue generally succeeds, though occasionally the banter feels constructed rather than natural. The ending strikes the right tone - neither falsely optimistic nor genuinely dark, but maintaining the characters' resilient pessimism that defines good post-apocalyptic humor. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Scene: “The Last Chapter Bookshop, Aberystwyth”** The bell above the door clattered like a startled seagull. Cai Vaughan, star of the *Crown of Thorns* saga and three consecutive “Most Desirable Man” polls, slipped inside, pressed his back to the door, and exhaled. His flat cap and sunglasses were useless. A pack of photographers had cornered him two streets down, outside a café that sold, allegedly, the best Welsh rarebit in the county. He hadn’t even gotten a bite. “Closed,” said a voice from behind a tower of Penguins. Cai blinked. The shop was a labyrinth of sagging shelves, dust motes doing a slow waltz in the single shaft of light, and the smell of old paper and rain. “It’s 2:47,” he said, checking his watch. “Your sign says open.” “The sign lies.” A woman emerged. She was mid-thirties, with a thick auburn plait over one shoulder and a cardigan that had seen better decades. She held a stack of hardbacks against her chest like a shield. “We’re closed for inventory. Also, you’re him. The film bloke.” Cai’s practiced grin flickered on—the one that had melted a thousand hearts on red carpets. “Cai Vaughan. And you are… the oracle of all things printed?” “Bronwen.” She didn’t smile. “And the oracle is currently counting unsold copies of your autobiography. *My Truth, My Light*. We’ve had it in the window for three months. It’s the only book in the shop that’s gathering dust faster than the *Encyclopaedia of Welsh Fungi*.” The grin faltered. He stepped closer, drifting past a display of local poetry. “That’s a shame. I signed a hundred of those. Thought they’d fly off the shelves.” “They flew off the shelf into the bargain bin,” Bronwen said, setting the stack down with a decisive thud. “I’m not trying to be rude. It’s just… you’re interrupting my counting. And you’re hiding.” Cai’s ego, that fragile, pampered creature, gave a small whimper. He’d expected gasps. Or at least a nervous laugh. Instead, this woman was looking at him like he was a overdue library book. He leaned against a shelf, adopting his most charming, lopsided pose. “Hiding? I’m *strategically relocating*. The paparazzi outside are like wolves. And you, my dear, are a very sturdy-looking cabin.” “I’m not your cabin. And it’s Bronwen, not ‘my dear’.” She tucked a stray hair behind her ear. Her fingers were stained with ink. “You can stay. But you have to help. Alphabetize the ‘C’ section. Someone’s put *Cooking with Coal* next to *Cormac McCarthy*.” He laughed—a real one, surprised out of him. “You’re joking.” “Do I look like I’m joking?” She gestured to a trolley of books. “Those aren’t going to sort themselves, Mr. Vaughan.” He peeled off his sunglasses, tucking them into his jacket. His eyes, famously described as “oceanic” by *Vanity Fair*, met hers. He expected a flicker. She just raised an eyebrow. “Fine,” he said, picking up a copy of *The Road*. “But I warn you, I’m a method actor. I’ll need to get into the mindset of a disgruntled librarian. That means brooding. And possibly sighing loudly.” “You’ll fit right in,” Bronwen said, turning back to her stack. But he caught it—the faintest twitch at the corner of her mouth. A crack in the fortress. They worked in silence for a minute. Cai slid books into place, his fingers brushing the spines. It was oddly calming. No cameras. No flashing. Just the rustle of paper and the occasional creak of the old floorboards. “You know,” he said, “most people want a selfie. Or an autograph. You just want me to file *Proust* under ‘P’.” “I want you to file *Proust* under ‘Proust’,” she corrected. “And you’re not most people. You’re the bloke who played the pirate captain. My nephew cried when you died. I told him it was acting. He didn’t believe me.” Cai’s chest puffed slightly. “That’s a compliment. I made him feel something.” “You made him think you were actually dead for three days. He wore black to school.” She finally looked at him, full on. Her eyes were the color of the sea before a storm. “You’re very good at pretending.” The words landed like a paper cut—sharp, unexpected, and stinging. He set down a copy of *Middlemarch* and turned to face her fully. “And what are you pretending, Bronwen? That you don’t know exactly who I am? That you didn’t see *The Last Voyage* three times in the cinema?” Her cheeks flushed—a betraying rose. She busied herself with a receipt book. “Once. And it was for the cinematography.” “Liar,” he said softly, and something in his voice made her look up. The charm had dropped, just for a second, leaving something rawer underneath. “I’m good at pretending. That’s the job. But I’m not good at being alone. And when the cameras stop, that’s all I am. Alone. In a hotel room. Ordering room service for one.” Bronwen’s hands stilled. She felt the flutter in her chest—the one she’d been suppressing since he walked in. She’d seen every interview. Every late-night show. She knew his laugh was rehearsed. But this—this wasn’t. “Why are you telling me this?” she asked, quieter now. He shrugged, a ghost of his rogue’s grin returning. “Because you’re the first person in a week who hasn’t tried to feed my ego. It’s starving. And you’re the only one offering something real.” She laughed—a short, surprised sound. “I offered you alphabetizing.” “Exactly.” He stepped closer. Not predatory, but tentative. “My last girlfriend—Sofia, the model—she left me a note. Said I was ‘exhausting’ because I needed everyone to love me. And she was right. I do. I need it like air. But you look at me like I’m just… a man with a book. And it’s terrifying. And I don’t want to leave.” Bronwen’s heart was doing something absurd. She clutched a copy of *Jane Eyre* to her chest. “You don’t even know me.” “I know you don’t like my autobiography. I know you alphabetize with military precision. I know your hands smell like paper and you bite your lip when you’re nervous.” He nodded at her mouth. “You’re doing it now.” She dropped the book. “That’s—that’s observation, not knowing.” “It’s a start.” He held out his hand. “Cai Vaughan. Unemployed actor, currently hiding from four men with telephoto lenses, and hoping to buy a cup of tea from the most intimidating woman in Wales.” She stared at his hand. Then, slowly, she took it. Her palm was warm, slightly rough. “Bronwen Rees. Bookshop owner. And I don’t have tea. But I have instant coffee and a kettle that’s older than you.” “Perfect,” he said, and his smile was genuine—no cameras, no audience. Just for her. “I hate tea anyway.” She laughed, finally, a real one. “You’re a disaster, Cai Vaughan.” “I know,” he said. “But I’m your disaster. At least until the wolves give up.” And for the first time that afternoon, neither of them was pretending.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a Welsh setting (Aberystwyth bookshop) and establishes the core dynamic between Cai, a famous actor with a fragile ego, and Bronwen, a bookshop owner who appears immune to his charm. The dialogue-driven approach works well, with each character maintaining distinct voices throughout. The characterization is particularly effective. Cai's desperation for validation comes through authentically - his practiced charm faltering when met with Bronwen's indifference creates genuine tension. His vulnerability about being "alone" and "exhausting" feels earned rather than manipulative. Bronwen's character is well-balanced; her resistance to his charm feels natural rather than contrived, while her gradual warming (the "betraying rose" blush, her knowledge of his films) shows internal conflict without betraying her established personality. The prose quality is generally high, with effective imagery like "dust motes doing a slow waltz" and "ego, that fragile, pampered creature." The Welsh setting feels authentic without being heavy-handed. The pacing builds naturally from initial antagonism to tentative connection. However, there are some weaknesses. The transformation feels slightly rushed - Cai's shift from practiced charm to genuine vulnerability happens quite quickly, though it's somewhat justified by Bronwen's unique resistance to his usual tactics. Some metaphors border on overwrought ("oceanic" eyes, "fortress" imagery). The ending, while sweet, edges toward convenient resolution. The dialogue is the piece's strongest element - each character speaks distinctively, and their verbal sparring feels natural and charged with subtext. The chemistry builds believably through their exchanges about books, his autobiography's poor sales, and their gradual revelation of mutual interest. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in the underhold was wrong. It was too still, too dry, as if the very dust had been told to hold its breath. Aya’s torch cast a sickly orange halo across flagstones that should have been slick with the damp of the harbour’s breath, but were instead as clean as a chapel floor. Behind her, Katra’s knife was already out, a whisper of steel against leather. Simeon’s breathing was a ragged counterpoint to the silence, his usual japery extinguished. “It’s a tomb,” Katra muttered, her voice a low growl. “I don’t like it.” Aya didn’t answer. Her skin prickled, the immateria humming just beneath her consciousness, a cold current waiting to be tapped. The door to the vault—a monstrosity of blackened oak and iron bands—stood before them. The scythan artifact, the *Heart of the Tides*, was a step beyond. She reached for the iron ring, her gloved fingers tingling. The ring turned without resistance. The door swung inward on silent, well-oiled hinges. And the quiet shattered. The vault was not a vault. It was a throne room. Candles, hundreds of them, guttered in iron sconces, their flames dancing in a draught that smelled of salt and old blood. And in the centre, seated on a crate of contraband rum, was the guild leader. Margrave Elara Voss. She was not in a gaol cell. She was not even dishevelled. Her greatcoat was immaculate, its brass buttons gleaming like the eyes of serpents. A cigarillo smouldered between her fingers, and at her hip hung a cutlass that had likely tasted more than one traitor’s throat. Behind her, two hulking figures stood like statues carved from granite and gristle, their faces hidden behind leather masks, their hands resting on the pommels of wicked-looking boarding axes. “Well, well,” Voss said, exhaling a plume of smoke that curled toward the vaulted ceiling. “The little moth comes to steal the candle. And she’s brought her friends.” Aya’s hand dropped from the door. Her mind raced, but her face was a mask of porcelain calm. “Margrave. I’d heard you were… detained.” “Detained,” Voss repeated, savouring the word. “Aye, I was. For precisely as long as I needed to be. You see, child, a trap is only a trap if the prey doesn’t know it’s being baited. And you—” she rose, the crate groaning in protest, “—you walked in as pretty as you please.” Katra shifted, her blade catching the candlelight. “She’s one woman. We can take her.” Voss laughed, a low, throaty sound. “Oh, I do like the fierce ones. But you’re not here to take me, girl. You’re here to be taken.” The bodyguards moved. It was not a charge, but a glide—a terrible, deliberate inevitability. Simeon scrambled backward, his hands raised, but a meaty fist caught him across the jaw and he crumpled like a sack of coal. Katra lunged, but the other guard sidestepped her blade with a contemptuous ease, his arm snaking around her throat. She choked, her knife clattering to the stones. Aya’s hand went to her own blade, but she never drew it. Voss was before her in three strides, the cigarillo dropped and ground out beneath a boot heel. The guild leader’s hand closed around Aya’s wrist, and the pressure was a vice of iron. “Let’s see the face of the woman who thinks she can outplay me,” Voss murmured, and with her free hand, she tore the mask away. The cold air hit Aya’s cheeks. The world tilted. She felt the immateria surge, desperate and hungry, begging to be unleashed, but she forced it down. Not yet. Not here. Voss studied her face with the detached curiosity of a naturalist examining a new species of beetle. “Aya Marchetti. Daughter of the woman who danced with the dark and paid the piper. I knew your mother, you know. She had the same look in her eye. The look that says ‘I am smarter than the rope.’” She smiled, and it was not a kind smile. “The rope disagreed.” Aya’s throat was dry, but she forced her voice to remain steady. “You’ve made your point, Margrave. You’re not in gaol. You’ve caught us. What now? A bullet in the back of the head, tossed into the harbour with the other refuse?” Voss tilted her head. “Tempting. But you’re worth more than that. You’re worth a great deal more.” Aya’s mind was a whirlwind. The immateria coiled in her gut, a serpent waiting to strike, but she could not use it—not with Simeon unconscious and Katra gasping in a guard’s grip. She had to buy time. She had to talk. “You’re right,” Aya said, forcing a brittle smile. “I am worth more. I’m the daughter of House Marchetti. My father sits on the Merchant Council. He has ships, warehouses, contracts with the Admiralty. If you ransom me, you could buy a fleet.” Voss laughed again, but this time it was colder. “Your father disowned you the moment he heard you spent your evenings in the company of thieves, child. He’s already sent word to the constabulary to report you as a runaway. No ransom will come from that quarter.” Aya’s stomach dropped. Of course. Of course he had. The man was a coward who had watched his wife hang and done nothing. Why would he lift a finger for his daughter? “Then ransom me to the Guild of Alchemists,” Aya pressed, desperation creeping into her voice. “My knowledge of immateria is worth a fortune. I can summon things—things that would make your bodyguards weep. I can be an asset.” Voss stepped closer, her face inches from Aya’s own. The woman’s breath smelled of rum and cloves. “You think I don’t know what you are, little witch? You think I don’t know that your mother’s blood sings in your veins? I’ve seen what your kind can do. I’ve seen the things that crawl out of the dark when you call them.” She reached out and traced a finger along Aya’s jawline, a gesture that was almost tender. “And that’s precisely why I’m not going to kill you. You’re too dangerous to waste.” Aya’s heart hammered. “Then what?” Voss smiled, and it was the smile of a woman who has already won. “You’re going to work for me, child. You’re going to be my pet monster. And if you refuse—” she glanced at Katra, who was still struggling uselessly, “—I’ll have your friend’s tongue cut out and fed to the gulls. And then I’ll do the same to you, piece by piece, until you agree.” The distant foghorn sounded three times, mournful and low, rolling across the harbour like a funeral bell. Aya felt the immateria surge again, a cold tide rising in her chest, and for a moment—just a moment—she considered letting it loose. Let the dark things come. Let the vault fill with screams. But then she looked at Katra, at the defiance in her friend’s eyes, and she knew she couldn’t. Not yet. “I accept,” Aya whispered, the words tasting like ash. “I’ll work for you.” Voss clapped her hands together, a sound like a pistol shot. “Excellent! See? That wasn’t so hard.” She turned to her guards, jerking her chin toward the unconscious Simeon. “Take them to the lower cells. And bring the brandy. We have a new apprentice to toast.” As the guards dragged them away, Aya’s mind was a storm of fury and fear. She had walked into the heart of the guild expecting to claim power. Instead, she had walked into a cage of her own making. And somewhere in the dark, her mother’s ghost was laughing.
